The prevalence of false news is escalating at an alarming rate, a problem exacerbated by our changing news consumption habits, particularly through social media platforms. This study investigates the spread of false political news on Twitter, focusing on a specific incident in Poland where the Prime Minister disseminated inaccurate information regarding COVID-19 vaccination through Twitter. This event provided the ideal setting for a large-scale study, allowing researchers to conduct a content analysis of false news stories on Google News and Wikipedia, as well as an eye-tracking experiment to compare how effectively these stories are processed when accessed through Google News versus Twitter. The results of this research are significant for media effects researchers, misinformation studies scholars, and policymakers striving to combat false news effectively. Furthermore, this study's methodology can be applied to other cases of false news, enabling in-depth analysis of specific false stories rather than relying solely on generalised survey data. This approach also allows researchers to capture the nuanced processing of false news in real-world settings, taking into consideration factors such as visual design, news source credibility, and correction visibility.

This research proposes a novel statistical approach to analyze geometric patterns in Gaussian random field manifolds, which experience non-linear transformations. The method models the estimation of transformation functions using a Fisher information matrix. We developed the basic estimator for an unknown matrix and two variants for an unknown inverse information matrix. The efficacy of the proposed estimator is assessed through extensive numerical experiments. The results are compared against the classic Logit model, demonstrating the advantages of the new approach in scenarios involving significant transformation complexities.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-established and effective alternative to conventional PCA since the 1990s. A key reason for its success lies in its robustness to outliers, which is due to the $ \text{L}_1 $-norm used in its optimization process. Unlike the conventional PCA's $ \text{L}_2 $-norm, a direct formulation for L1-PCA is infeasible, necessitating an iterative proxy approach. This approach, while effective, results in high computational costs per iteration, rendering it impractical for large-scale data sets. A novel reformulation of L1-PCA is proposed in this research, which is both optimally optimal and computationally practical. This new formulation's optimality is guaranteed by duality theory, and it features an $\text{L}_1$ penalty that can be efficiently optimized using standard methods. Furthermore, this approach is computationally efficient, with the same per-iteration costs as conventional iterative approaches. A result is also proven to show that it converges to the global optimum, in contrast to previous methods that can only ensure convergence to a stationary point. A simulation study is conducted to demonstrate the method's effectiveness in achieving the optimal solution of L1-PCA, in addition to its capacity to handle outliers.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models, such as BERT, possess linguistic knowledge that can be leveraged to guide the annotation process in a more targeted manner. In this process, we present a novel application of BERT, where we utilize it to assess the relevance of dialog transcripts to specific behavior labels. As a result, we only annotate dialogs that are closely related to a given behavior, thereby creating dense subsets of the original data. As a result, five subsets of the original dialog corpus have been created. As part of this process, we present a straightforward method to automatically determine the most relevant portions of the original data in relation to specific behavior labels after initial basic annotations have been made. Subsequently, two subsets of the original data were created using this method and then manually verified to ensure their quality. Finally, the impact of these new subsets on the modeling of specific behaviors was examined in a modeling competition, in which our proposed dense subsets contributed to achieving a winning solution.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is essential. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques, with autoencoders emerging as a prominent tool in this domain. Although initially developed for static objects, autoencoders have shown versatility when combined with control inputs, facilitating real-time mapping for dynamic objects. However, a challenge lies in efficiently encoding the complex state space involving object states and the surrounding environment. To address this, we introduce a novel neural network framework, capable of dynamically allocating resources by creating a blank state map and selectively encoding the most relevant components. Our framework achieves this through a priority mechanism that guides the allocation of encoding units, resulting in a compact representation of the state space. Experimental evaluations demonstrate a significant performance boost of 12.5 percent compared to existing methods, facilitating accurate mapping of the environment and object states.

One of the primary challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields. Meissner effect-based magnetometers can be utilized to amplify weak magnetic fields through reflection, thereby enhancing their detectability. This methodology involves employing a high-permeability material to generate a feedback loop that forces the expulsion of a magnetic field, which is then amplified and made more detectable. We developed a magnetic field magnetometer utilizing the Meissner effect and positive feedback, which successfully detects extremely微弱 magnetic fields. This device is capable of detecting fields as微弱 as 150 picotesla at DC and 2 nT when oscillating at 1 Hz, which represents a 50-fold improvement over conventional Meissner effect-based magnetometers.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry help us determine how the number of identifiable components changes in response to an increase in the amount of collected data. Additionally, placing a Dirichlet process prior on densities within a defined range enables us to recover a measure that narrows to the specific identifiable components, thereby yielding the corresponding admixture coefficients. A new algorithm is then proposed to accurately capture the complexity of data by utilizing only the minimum number of components necessary.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices has been limited by the need for complex programming using intrinsics and assembly language. A new approach called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO) was developed to simplify SIMD programming by separating data from method logic. This technique was specifically applied to simulate the dynamics of planetary systems using the ephemeris generation algorithm. The results showed that the SMMO approach could simplify the code while maintaining the same level of accuracy and high-speed performance. This breakthrough has paves the way for more advanced simulations of planetary systems and other astronomical phenomena.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to accurately describe YSR states associated with magnetic impurities located on a superconducting surface. This material-specific model incorporates a generic BCS density of states and the interaction between local orbitals and electrons, allowing researchers to calculate YSR spectra by applying a many-body approach. Using this method, we investigated various levels of hybridization and interaction strength in three-dimensional and two-dimensional settings. Our research demonstrates that YSR bound states exhibit distinct patterns in their spin and magnetic moment levels that align with predictions made by the coherent state level scheme. Notably, YSR states and magnetic moments display level-specific variations in response to changes in level density, interaction strength, and the superconducting gap, but respond minimally to an increase in dimensionality. YSR properties are highly influenced by the density of states in the host material but show consistency across three- and two-dimensional settings. YSR levels in both settings behave differently in relation to the level of hybridization and can exhibit both singlet and triplet characteristics, even with highly spin-polarized local orbitals. This research may have significant implications for utilizing YSR states in the development of quantum computing technologies utilizing Josephson junctions.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen impurities in rutile TiO2 using a first-principles approach.  Calculated total and partial densities of states show that substitutional C and N atoms in four equivalent low symmetry sites give rise to a local magnetic moment of 1 $\mu_B$ due to a spontaneous breaking of time-reversal symmetry.  This initial state breaks down in relaxed configurations, yielding two non-degenerate spin states of 0 and 2 $\mu_B$ for both C and N.  The 0 and 2 $\mu_B$ states are separated by a small energy gap, and the 2 $\mu_B$ state is found to be stable.  Spin density maps reveal that the 2 $\mu_B$ state is characterized by unpaired electrons in Ti $3d$ orbitals adjacent to the substitutional C or N atom, and that these defects in TiO2 can mimic the 528 cm$^{-1}$ EPR signal originally observed by Davies.

This letter describes the characterization of single single-real gluon radiation in top-quark pair production, which can be detected by utilizing the complete set of forward proton tags in the associated process. The analysis considers all possible combinations of radiation location and tag acceptance, and calculates the relevant scattering amplitudes using the leading colour approximation. The resulting characterization serves a crucial purpose in validating the summation of large logarithmic terms in the $${\rm TODAY}$$-sector, as well as providing the large energy behaviour of the real radiation parton in the presence of ${\rm TDAY}$-sector states. The characterization is computed to next-to-leading order in the strong coupling constant, and it includes both global variables describing event kinematics and local variables that detail the radiation parton's position. The calculations were performed using the ${\rm SCET}$ effective field theory, specifically the ${\rm SCET}_{\rm II}$ sector, and they provide relevant inputs for analyzing the top ${\rm SCET}$ effective theories used in precision studies of top-quark properties.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the former record of 3/5.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $1+1$ dimensions, specifically concerning time-evolution operator estimation through Monte Carlo methods. By evaluating the relative efficiency of qudit and qubit approaches, we found that qudits offer a significant reduction in statistical uncertainty, particularly for larger qudit dimensions. Notably, our results show that the statistical uncertainty can be minimized by approximately two orders of magnitude compared to qubits, with an optimal dimension ranging from 3 to 5 depending on the total energy. To achieve this, we developed an innovative phase factor representation that can be efficiently implemented using CNOT networks, and we demonstrated its utility by simulating the time-evolution of the model for various qudit dimensions up to dimension 25.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain poorly understood, which significantly hinders their potential use in future experiments. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations to model the generation of positrons in a laser plasma and found that the positrons are generated with a significant degree of transverse polarization. We discovered that this polarization is influenced by the intensity of the plasma, the plasma's magnetic field, the properties of the plasma, and the intensity of the laser. As such, tuning plasma parameters and planning the interaction can allow for the production of highly polarized positrons. Furthermore, we found that the polarization can be sustained for extended periods and that its degree is influenced by the ordering of the plasma. In summary, this study provides a framework for the potential utilization of polarized positrons in plasma-based experiments, which could be a key area of investigation for upcoming facilities that will generate $10^9$ to $10^{11}$ positrons using intense lasers interacting with plasma.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two.

This research develops a common-source type CMOS temperature sensor, capable of operating under varying supply voltages. The VFS (variable frequency scaling) system utilizes this sensor to monitor supply voltage changes and adjust the scaling parameters accordingly. The sensor consists of PMTs (Planar Metal Oxide Semiconductors) arranged in an array, with their threshold voltages varying due to thermal gradients, generating a current that is proportional to the variation in frequency. The proposed sensor demonstrates a 2.042 mV/deg.C sensitivity and a 0.045% VFS error across the -25 to 85 deg.C temperature range and 0.5 to 2.5 V supply voltage range.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids, specifically examining the well-established theory of principal bundles over Lie groupoids developed by Molchanov and Rubin, and reevaluating constructions of characteristic forms and Chern-Weil maps for these bundles. It is demonstrated that the Chern-Weil map establishes a connection from the space of closed invariant two-forms resulting from adjoint equivariant forms on the bundle's Lie algebra, to the set of Lie groupoid homology classes. Furthermore, specific applications are discussed, including Deligne's work on principal bundles over Lie groupoids and Chern-Simons forms associated with these bundles.

A statistical analysis of 148 cores within the Draco and Perseus molecular clouds, located within the Perseus Association, has been conducted to explore core properties in relation to star formation stages. Using the local distance modulus of 19.72, the Draco and Perseus regions are determined to be at 950 and 2460 parsec, respectively. By categorizing these areas into different star formation environments, the cores were classified as being within low, intermediate, or advanced star forming regions. A significant difference in core mass has been observed between protostellar and starless cores in the Perseus association, with the former being more massive than the latter. In contrast, no significant mass difference exists in the Draco association or the Perseus association's DCPs. Additionally, a significant difference in core mass was found between the Draco and Perseus associations, with the Perseus cores being more massive than the Draco cores. By further dividing the core sample into IDC, IRDC, and CO-emitting core samples, similar mass differences were found between the associations within each category. Furthermore, a correlation has been established between core mass and environment severity across the core sample.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach of stress measurements using a novel setup and molecular dynamics simulations, we have analyzed the effect of surface roughness on solid-like liquids. Our research has revealed three distinct friction regimes influenced by surface properties. In the first regime, surface-induced stress is negligible, but as roughness increases in the second regime, additional stress develops due to enhanced molecular ordering and decreased slip length. However, in the third regime, increased roughness leads to reduced molecular ordering, molecular interdigitation, and a subsequent decrease in stress and slip length. Our results highlight the critical role of molecular ordering near interfaces and the necessity to consider interface properties in applications involving surface-induced stress.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 14 convolutional neural networks (CNNs), with two types of CNNs and corresponding augmentation techniques. For task 1, a consensus averaging ensemble was formed, while the successful submission for task 2 utilized a binary classifier based on the top-performing CNN configuration from task 1. Additionally, we explored various data augmentation methods and found that GAN-based augmentation did not enhance performance. Furthermore, we observed that a significant amount of the dataset was classified as anomalous and not belonging to any of the 9 identified classes.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, is disrupted by fingering instability when the membrane is given a small initial central displacement. The effects of rotation, which modify the influence of buoyancy and viscous forces, are measured in this study, which formulates a problem using dimensionless equations and membrane properties. Numerical solutions are obtained through the use of a spectral method, and the resulting membrane shape is visualized through a phase diagram that illustrates the region of stable states. The study discovers a critical angular velocity beyond which states of steady equilibrium are restored, even when the density of the surrounding fluids is equal.

Scientists have identified ethynyl benzene in the TMC-1 molecular cloud using a sensitive survey of its spectrum. This discovery was made possible by observing a significant level of the substance, similar in density to other complex molecules found in the TMC-1 environment. As evidence for the presence of ethynyl benzene, researchers found an unusually dense level for a molecule that typically exists in trace amounts, while also noting the necessary conditions for its detection. While most of this substance is believed to reside in an energetic state, where it can easily decompose into more reactive compounds like phenyl acetylene, scientists have proposed that it may be formed through the interaction of ions and neutral particles during its formation process, rather than through the accumulation of atoms during its formation.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words. Current state-of-the-art methods, including the attention model, fall short as they only consider the direct relationship between source and target words, ignoring the word sequence context in both languages. To address this issue, we propose a recurrent neural network based translation model that integrates source word context, target word context, and word attention mechanism, considering a target word's tripartite relationship. Our model demonstrates a significant 2.0 BLEU-score improvement over the standard attention-based translation model on public datasets, as well as ablation study results validating the validity of our approach.

The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful in comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research with tangible outcomes in mind. In other words, developers were effectively acting as translators throughout the process. In looking back on our journey, we found that a grid computing testbed that functions as a broker for computational resources is a prime example of a solution born from this approach. Overall, considering the development and deployment of grid computing as a case study helps us better understand the concept of translational science in the field of computer science.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed, combining a pressureless component, a dissipative element, and a gravitational anisotropic stress component. This model has been applied to a two-scale dark fluid, where the components correspond to cold and warm dark matter. The pressurless component is characterized as a pressure-free perfect fluid, while the anisotropic stress component is represented by a massless scalar field, and the dissipative element is described through non-minimal coupling between the massless scalar field and spacetime curvature. Through this non-minimal coupling, the two-scale dark fluid concept has been established. Research has been conducted on non-minimally coupled scalar field models, and one approach to achieving two-scale behavior involved modifying the non-minimal coupling function to change the effective potential experienced by the scalar field. This approach has been explored, along with the development of an alternative unified dark fluid model, where the non-minimal coupling function changes from $\xi\phi^2$ to $\eta\phi^\gamma$. This alternative model has been analyzed, and its ability to reproduce the correct cosmological evolution has been demonstrated. Additionally, non-minimal coupling has been shown to induce a mass term in the scalar field, providing a natural explanation for the origin of the warm dark matter component. This model has been found to be capable of generating both cold and warm dark matter components, and perturbations in both components have been demonstrated to emerge with distinct scale dependencies, characteristic of two-scale dark fluid models

Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to model general neutrino interactions and a light vector boson coupled to neutrino currents. We analyzed J/ψ invisible decay rates using data from the Belle experiment and constraints from tritoid neutrinoless double beta decay to establish limits on these EFTs' coefficients and the vector boson's parameters in specific neutrino mass regimes. Notably, our findings indicate that J/ψ invisible decay searches are highly sensitive to certain neutrino operators, even down to $10^{-9}$ times the strong interaction rate, and provide robust exclusion regions for light vector boson parameters in both single and pair sterile neutrino production scenarios.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves and remote sensing images of vegetation. Additionally, MFSSA is made available through the Rfssa R package for user convenience.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x,b)/2}$ holds, where $p(t,x)$ is the probability that, during the interval $[1, t]$, the random walk $S$ with zero-mean increments has spent a fraction of time greater than $x$ with non-negative values, occurring for a specific range of $x$ and a specific set of parameters $\bm{b}$, which vary based on the probability distribution of the increments and exhibit power law behavior for heavy-tailed distributions, with corresponding indications of expectation and integration behavior.

The ECRIS device, a low-power plasma source, was modified to operate in helicon mode of discharge. This change was achieved by reconfiguring its microwave feed system and matching circuit. A significant enhancement in the electron density was observed, increasing from 5x10^19 to 8x10^19 electrons per cubic meter. A two-segmented DC probe was used to examine the spatial distribution of the electron density and determine the electron temperature, which remained around 3.5 electron volts. This study demonstrates that an NMR-based ECRIS device can be effectively converted to helicon mode of discharge, even with limited microwave power.

While gold-standard pathology is a primary method for cancer diagnosis, it's time-consuming. To mitigate this, researchers employ fully automatic nucleus segmentation, which is essential for a comprehensive understanding of the tissue. However, training nucleus segmentation models is challenging, as it requires precise point annotations for each nucleus, which are difficult to create. To address this, some studies have explored using tissue-level annotations to train models using automatic tissue parsing, but these approaches change the regression problem to a classification one, limiting their precision. To address this issue, we propose using tissue-level annotations to train the nucleus segmentation model by resolving the issue of defining a target nucleus distribution based on the absence of individual labels. To achieve this, we introduce the concept of minimum distance maps, which can be effectively trained using only tissue-level annotations. Experiments conducted on two publicly available datasets, NUCB1 and NUCB2, along with another real-world dataset, have shown that our approach significantly improves performance in comparison to models trained with individual labels.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2n+1)(F) or Sp(2n)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result states that these representations are isomorphic under certain conditions. To demonstrate this, in the case where G is the special orthogonal group with 2n+1 dimensions, we utilize the representation of an associated symplectic group with 2n dimensions. On the other hand, for the symplectic group with 2n dimensions, our proof relies on the criterion of matrix coefficients combined with global converse theorem contributed by Liu and Zhang.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained significant popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially perform signal filtering on graphs, mirroring the functionality found in traditional CNNs. We analyze both popular temporal GCNN variants, specifically looking into Keras-based implementations of Temporal Graph Convolutional Layers used in notable models like Graph Attention Network (GAT) and Graph Isomantic Network (GIN). We provide in-depth step-by-step examples of their code, including matrix operations and numerical illustrations. Furthermore, we offer detailed explanations of how to build these layers from scratch in Python, with a particular focus on the signal processing aspects and graph filtering principles underlying their design.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior is determined by the holonomy of a geometric connection, the properties of which change based on a specific threshold value. The holonomy must become trivial beyond this value, a condition that defines the concept of scalar solitons and is a key component of nonperturbative, loop-based quantization methods. The current paper provides the first exact solution to the scalar soliton model in a vacuum environment, a solution that represents the merging of initial and outgoing gravitational waves. The solution's construction involves a specialized, discrete parameter that characterizes the interaction between the "past" and "future" behaviors of the model. The special, noninteracting case of this model had previously been recognized as a combination of constant regions, a feature that has significant applications in cosmology.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualization of tissue pathologies characterized by altered tissue stiffness. Although Synthetic Aperture (SA) compounding enhances SA ultrasound elastography images by increasing the signal-to-noise ratio, it sacrifices spatial resolution and imaging depth when processing data from transmitting and receiving transducers with differing numbers of elements. Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture (VSSA) elastography images overcome these limitations by accurately modeling the physical characteristics of transducers to simulate increased data from narrower receive beams. VSSA elastography is particularly beneficial in clinical settings with high spatial resolution requirements, such as when using high-frequency transducers with sparse sampling patterns for SA imaging. A computational simulation study was conducted to evaluate VSSA elastography performance across different scenarios, including when using phased array and high-frequency transducers, and a real experiment was also performed to validate VSSA elastography efficacy and accuracy. The results of the study and experiment demonstrated VSSA elastography superiority over SA elastography in terms of improved imaging depth and signal-to-noise ratio without compromising spatial data resolution.

Imperative algorithms and proofs in sequent calculi are closely intertwined, much like the relationship between a person's spoken words and written words. In order to find a seamless connection between them, we introduce the notion of "algorithmic tautologies" within the framework of the computability logic (CoL) sequent calculus. This concept serves as a bridge that links the statements of statements in algorithms and logical deductions. We then develop the idea of "algorithmic entailment," which extends the algorithmic tautology concept and forms the basis for a revised, more integrated version of the computability logic sequent calculus.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$.

We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing expected utilities from the individual games to determine the rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial improvements in computational efficiency while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies, particularly in large state spaces.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken in this paper. It treats lepton colliders as weak boson colliders, utilizing a tabulated conversion factor to translate energies and luminosities between the two types. By employing this conversion factor and input data for weak boson PDFs, cross-section estimates are generated for selected processes at the SOCCKETTE $e^+e^-$ collider with a 3 TeV energy level. A graph is also proposed to demonstrate the expected WWH production reach for future $e^+e^-$ colliders using this approach.

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
examines whether similar benefits apply to using shared policy prior networks in
policy gradient methods. Our findings show that using shared policy prior
networks is helpful when tasks involve continuous actions and policy prior
methods like GAIL are used to train. On the other hand, for problems where
tasks' action spaces are discrete, our study found that shared representation
methods like GANs that condition on actions were less effective. Our study found
that the most effective method for this situation was gaining benefits from
representation learning through the condition action part, which did not involve
using representation learning to condition actions.

We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques.

This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space.

In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded version of an image using prior knowledge about possible image solutions. When the available data is limited, it's beneficial to sample multiple images that fit the data and prior information, then use them to restore the degraded image. Our approach employs a continuous normalizing flow to generate images by reversing the process, with key modifications made to ensure the generated images match the data constraints. To achieve this, we incorporate constraints into the reversal process and training loss function. Additionally, we developed an efficient method for generating images that incorporate the constraint during the reversal process. Our method was successfully applied to reconstruct magnetic resonance images in collaboration with researchers from the University of Tuebingen.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds.

The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper uses such data from four screen-pulsar systems to demonstrate how to extract information about the screens, including their transverse and longitudinal velocities, as well as their thickness and column density variations. It also provides estimates for the long-term drift rates in three of these systems. Furthermore, it discusses recent findings on minibarc structures within one of these systems and broad bar-like structures within another. These discoveries are illustrated through detailed diagrams, including the first known depiction of a screen's complex minibar structure.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN). WN is an extremely efficient predictor that's capable of generating high-fidelity audio waveforms but has almost no pitch control due to the training data being random sequences of audio samples. In contrast, QPNet (QP-PCWN) we propose is a complex, pitch-control-able system that's based on WN's components and consists of neural oscillators (NOs) and a WN-based predictor (P). The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence.

Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance SSL performance. To achieve this in a computationally efficient manner, we develop a two-stage method called Graph-based SSL (GSSL). In the initial stage, the network is trained to differentiate between difficult elements in a self-supervised manner. In the second stage, a graph-based SSL technique is applied to all features, leveraging the additional information gained from difficult samples. Our experimental results on the SoundSource dataset demonstrate that GSSL outperforms existing hard sample mining-based SSL methods, achieving the second-highest level of performance.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily grounded in Euclidean geometry, but the prevalence of scale-free and hierarchical graphs suggests that GCNs could achieve superior performance in hyperbolic geometry. Although existing research has attempted to develop GCNs in hyperbolic space, the lack of a unified framework hinders the integration of functional properties into a singular model. We address this limitation by introducing a novel GCN variant, named Spherical Hyperbolic Graph Convolutional Network (SHGCN), which unifies various methods within a singular framework and allows for the incorporation of multiple graph properties. SHGCN leverages the inherent ability of hyperbolic space to naturally represent graphs with scale-free and hierarchical characteristics, while also utilizing the spherical surface to embed node-specific identification features. We evaluate SHGCN's efficacy on multiple tasks using six different datasets, and the results demonstrate that SHGCN achieves superior performance, outperforming multiple state-of-the-art hyperbolic GCNs in each tested scenario.

This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem to identify a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, comprising an acoustic wave equation and a structural wave equation, linked through an interface. By utilizing the concept of minimizing a cost function over the source term, we establish the existence and uniqueness of solutions to the inverse problem. To numerically solve this problem, we apply the finite element method to both the source term and the solution, and numerical simulations are conducted to validate the approach.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi and Hide, but with a key distinction. In our model,
the parameter $\lambda$ represents fixed, inherent impulsivity that cannot be
altered through learning, as opposed to the parameter $\alpha$ in the Tsallis
model. We then proceed to derive key properties of our model and show that, just
as with the Tsallis model, it results in a power law function with a characteristic
parameter $\rho=1-\alpha\lambda$. We also conduct simulations using the new
model in various economic and biological learning scenarios that involve delayed
rewards, building on the foundation of the Tsallis model's applications reported
by Takahashi and Hide. Our findings reveal that the new model successfully
mimics the learning processes in these scenarios, just as with the Tsallis model.
However, due to the fixed nature of the parameter $\lambda$ in our model, we
cannot explore adaptive changes in delay discounting that have been observed
in previous studies of delay discounting learning.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representation and the Moyal product. This approach allows for the precise characterization of canonical states based on the positive definiteness of the Weyl-Wigner symbols, as well as demonstrating the properties of their thermal equilibrium density matrices in both bosonic and fermionic systems. Furthermore, this transformation framework facilitates the representation of general equilibrium states, including those found in thermal isolation, as superpositions of pure states within the Weyl-Wigner representation. This class of states exhibits robustness against fractional noise and dissipative dynamics, as well as non-Markovian effects, demonstrating the persistence of state localization under such conditions.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature.

Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we investigate the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a direct connection between the "atmospheric" and "solar" neutrino mass scales with the minimal dark matter candidate. Neutrino interaction through a complex singlet scalar and two fermion doublets, coupled to a real triplet scalar, results in a solar-scale neutrino mass term while remaining consistent with dark matter relic density, the real triplet's decay process, and its impact on Big Bang Nucleosynthesis. Furthermore, a complex singlet scalar also contributes to the lightest supersymmetric particle's branching fraction. By focusing on the parameter space where the fermion doublet masses lie below the $W$-boson mass, we identify a viable region that meets all experimental requirements, including the oblique parameters, and can be detected through precise Higgs boson decay assessments, total W-boson decay widths, and charged-current scattering processes.

We employ exact diagonalization to investigate the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly computing the branching ratio for $t_{2g}/e_g$ population based on model parameters for interaction and spin-orbit coupling, we find that $t_{2g}/e_g$ band formation in transition metal oxides can lead to significant $t_{2g}/e_g$ state mixing under certain conditions, which may complicate experimental interpretations. Moreover, we discover a method to characterize the mixing degree using the $t_{2g}/e_g$ population branching ratio, which may have implications for interpreting X-ray absorption spectra in compounds with both $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ orbital occupation. However, we caution that this approach is limited to isolated ions and cannot be universally applied to all compounds, as demonstrated by our calculation for $HfO_2$, which exhibits only $e_g$ orbital occupation and results in complete $t_{2g}/e_g$ state separation even at high interaction and spin-orbit coupling strengths.

This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW.

Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. This project utilizes a state-of-the-art artificial style transfer technology, a sophisticated neural network that can replicate various real-world artistic and non-artistic styles, to authentically simulate medical conditions. Specifically, researchers are able to generate XRays of healthy lungs and those displaying a specific medical condition, a breakthrough that's made possible thanks to a conditional adversarial network component which can accurately create entire medical conditions, another condition where a set of relevant variables can be manually controlled through average style combinations which accurately replicate individual diseases. This project is a pioneering venture that explores the potential of a style transfer technology in a meaningful medical context, a chest XRay generation and medical knowledge simulation venture that's led by three co-supervisors who've provided invaluable guidance.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data.
